facts.fact_text: On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.
The march on 11 June 2005 followed the itinerary as planned in the original request of 12 May 2005.
The march on 11 June 2005 was attended by approximately 3,000 people.
On 3 June 2005 the Traffic Officer, acting on behalf of the Mayor of Warsaw, refused permission for the march.

The Traffic Officer's refusal of permission for the march on 3 June 2005 was based on the organisers' failure to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') within the meaning of Article 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act.
The Traffic Officer alleged that the organisers had been ordered to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') prior to the refusal of 3 June 2005.
On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.

Under section 65 of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, the organisers of sporting events, contests, assemblies and other events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to obtain permission for the organisation of such assemblies.

Under section 65 read together with section 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, organisers of events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to comply with various administrative obligations specified in a list contained in section 65(a), numbering nineteen items, including the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan to the authorities.
The provisions of sections 65 and 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, were repealed as a result of the judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006.

In its judgment of 18 January 2006, the Constitutional Court examined a request submitted by the Ombudsman to determine whether the requirements imposed on organisers of public events by the provisions of the Road Traffic Act were compatible with the Constitution in so far as they impinged on freedom of assembly, or whether they amounted to an excessive limitation of that freedom.

The Constitutional Court observed that the essence of the constitutional problem was whether the requirements imposed by section 65 of the Road Traffic Act were compatible with freedom of expression as formulated by the Constitution and developed by the 1990 Assemblies Act.
The Constitutional Court noted that the 1990 Assemblies Act was based on the premise that the exercise of freedom of assembly did not require any authorisations or licences issued by the State.

The Constitutional Court noted that freedom of assembly being a freedom meant the State was obliged to refrain from hindering its exercise and to ensure that it was enjoyed by various groups despite the fact that their views might not be shared by the majority.
The Constitutional Court observed that the 1990 Assemblies Act provided for a system based on nothing more than the registration of the proposed assembly.

The Constitutional Court observed that when the legislature enacted the Road Traffic Act, it incorporated various administrative requirements which were difficult to comply with into the procedure created for the organisation of sporting events, contests and assemblies, thus replacing the registration system by a system based on permission.

The Constitutional Court observed that the Road Traffic Act placed assemblies within the meaning of the 1990 Assemblies Act on a par with events of a commercial character or organised for entertainment purposes.

The Constitutional Court found that placing assemblies on a par with commercial or entertainment events was incompatible with the special position that freedom of expression occupied in a democratic society and rendered nugatory the special place that assemblies had in the legal system under the Constitution and the 1990 Assemblies Act.
The Constitutional Court noted that the list of requirements imposed by the Road Traffic Act contained as many as nineteen sundry administrative obligations.

The Constitutional Court found that the restrictions on freedom of assembly imposed by the Road Traffic Act were in breach of the requirement of proportionality applicable to all restrictions imposed on the rights guaranteed by the Constitution.
The Constitutional Court concluded in its judgment of 18 January 2006 that section 65 of the Road Traffic Act was incompatible with the Constitution in so far as it applied to assemblies.

In his decision of 9 June 2005 banning the stationary assemblies, the Mayor of Warsaw relied on the argument that assemblies held under the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act (Ustawa o zgromadzeniach) had to be organised away from roads used for road traffic.
The Mayor of Warsaw refused permission for the applicants' stationary assemblies in part to avoid possible violent clashes between participants in the various demonstrations planned for 11 June 2005.

The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw's reliance on the threat of violence between the demonstrations organised by the applicants and the counter-demonstrations planned by other persons and organisations for 11 June 2005 could not be countenanced.

The Mazowsze Governor stated that the Mayor of Warsaw's reliance on the threat of violence was tantamount to the administration endorsing the intentions of organisations which clearly and deliberately intended to breach public order.
